title: Citi instant payments go live as Australia's surcharge ban bites
summary: Citi activates multi-market instant cross-border payments via Swift in October 2026, raising real AML control questions. Plus Australia's card surcharge ban lands, and two overdue obligations demand attention from HK and Singapore compliance leads.
script:
ALEX: Citi flipped the switch this week on multi-market instant payments through Swift's instant payments scheme, and I want to start there, because this is not a product story. It is a controls story. Jordan, how are you reading it?

JORDAN: I'm reading it as a Monday morning problem for transaction monitoring teams across the region. The moment you settle cross-border payments in near-real time, the detection window collapses. Your rules were calibrated for batch settlement cycles. They were not calibrated for this.

ALEX: Right, and the specific operational tension is that your correspondent-banking due diligence model, your derisking logic, your threshold alerts, all of that was built assuming you had hours, sometimes an overnight window, to intervene before a payment completed. Instant settlement removes that buffer almost entirely.

JORDAN: And it's not just the detection window. It's the data quality at the point of origination. If a corporate treasury client can push a payment across three or four jurisdictions in seconds, the beneficiary verification, the sanctions screening, all of that has to be completed upstream before the instruction hits the rails. You cannot screen after the fact on an irrevocable instant payment.

ALEX: So the supervisory read here, from where I sit, is that HKMA, MAS, and AUSTRAC are all going to treat this as an infrastructure change that requires a control change notification, or at minimum a program review trigger. MAS Notice 626 already requires quarterly governance reviews of STR processes, and I think any institution that has onboarded Citi's instant payment rails without updating its transaction monitoring calibration is carrying an undocumented gap.

JORDAN: I'll push back slightly on the MAS framing. Notice 626's quarterly STR governance obligation is a filing and escalation review, not a controls adequacy review. The instrument you want is the annual AML and CTF program review. And for Australian institutions, that is actually Section 84 of the AML/CTF Act, which requires an annual board-level review and sign-off on both Part A and Part B of the program. If your program does not address real-time payment risk, your board approval is signing off on something that is already out of date.

ALEX: That is fair. The Section 84 review is the right hook in Australia. What should listeners actually do with this before end of week?

JORDAN: Three things. First, if you are the MLRO at any institution that has enabled or is piloting instant cross-border payment flows, pull your transaction monitoring calibration documentation today and confirm whether the detection logic addresses sub-minute settlement windows. If it doesn't, that goes to your risk committee before month-end. Second, confirm that your sanctions screening is embedded in the pre-authorisation step, not post-settlement. Third, raise with your technology and operations counterpart whether your current Swift connectivity for this scheme includes an automatic hold or flag capability for high-risk corridors. If the answer is no, that is a gap you need to document and escalate now.

ALEX: All of that is practical. I'd add one supervisory note. Regulators across this region have been consistently critical of institutions that adopt new payment infrastructure without a commensurate update to their risk assessments. The HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline at paragraph 11, which is the same paragraph that anchored the annual self-assessment return that was due on the thirtieth of September, specifically calls out ongoing monitoring adequacy as a live obligation, not just an annual one. If you are in Hong Kong and you filed your self-assessment return this week without noting an open gap on instant payment controls, that is a document you may need to revisit.

JORDAN: Which brings me to something I want to flag to Hong Kong compliance leads directly. The HKMA's Q4 2025 thematic review of STR narrative quality is still carrying open deficiency letters for roughly twenty-five percent of the authorised institution population. Those closure obligations are now five months overdue from their April deadline. I know some teams have been deprioritising this because it feels like a documentation exercise. It is not. If HKMA comes in for a follow-up visit and finds that your deficiency response is still outstanding, your self-assessment return filed last Tuesday becomes exhibit one in a supervisory conversation you do not want to have.

ALEX: And the self-assessment return is not a sealed document. Examiners read it against your thematic review correspondence. If you said in your self-assessment that STR governance is adequate, but your deficiency response to the Q4 thematic is still sitting incomplete, that is a direct inconsistency that examiners will surface.

JORDAN: So if you are a head of financial crime compliance at an HKMA-regulated institution and you have an open deficiency letter, the action is not to draft a better response. It is to close the actual finding, which means fixing the narrative quality in your STR templates, evidencing the retraining of your analysts, and getting a sign-off from your MLRO that the control is remediated. Then you write the response. Documentation of a fixed problem, not documentation in place of fixing it.

ALEX: Moving on briefly to Australia. The card surcharge ban that took effect on the first of October is getting a lot of consumer press, and the Australian Banking Association's chief executive Simon B has been doing the media rounds explaining the consumer benefit. But there is a quiet compliance implication that is not making those headlines.

JORDAN: Yes, and it's this. When you remove surcharges, you change consumer payment routing incentives. People shift toward higher-interchange card products. That is a volume and mix shift for acquiring banks, and it affects the transaction patterns that your AML systems were trained on. It probably doesn't move the needle for most institutions this week, but if you are running a risk-based approach that uses transaction-type profiling, this is worth noting in your next model review cycle.

ALEX: I'd also flag it for payment facilitators operating across Australia. The compliance burden on acquiring institutions is real, and where there is operational pressure and margin compression, controls sometimes get deprioritised. That is a supervision risk, not just a business risk.

JORDAN: Agreed. And before we close, a quick reminder for Singapore compliance teams. The MAS Notice 626 quarterly STR governance review for the period ending June 2026 has been sitting on the overdue list since mid-July. If your institution has not completed and documented that review, that is the thing to fix before anything else this week. Pull the last quarter's STR filings, check completeness and timeliness, reconcile against STRO acknowledgements, and minute the output. That review needs a record.

ALEX: That's the week ahead. Instant payments infrastructure, STR remediation in Hong Kong, and a quiet but real payment-mix shift in Australia. The obligation register and source links for everything we've discussed today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. See you tomorrow.
